taxonomy.subtopic: Heteroplasmy, replicative segregation, and tissue-specific threshold effect

questions.stem_html: A woman with mild sensorineural hearing loss has two children with the same pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant. One child has only exercise intolerance, whereas the other develops seizures, lactic acidosis, and cardiomyopathy. Testing shows different proportions of mutant mitochondrial DNA in skeletal muscle, myocardium, and blood among the three family members. Which mechanism best explains the variation in severity?

options.text_html: Random segregation of mutant and normal mitochondria produces tissue-specific heteroplasmy that may cross a functional threshold
Progressive expansion of a nuclear trinucleotide repeat causes anticipation
Paternal transmission of mitochondrial DNA creates different compound heterozygous genotypes
Random X-chromosome inactivation produces cellular mosaicism in both sons and daughters
Parent-of-origin methylation silences the maternal allele in selected tissues

questions.explanation_html: Cells contain many mitochondrial DNA copies. A pathogenic variant may coexist with normal mitochondrial DNA, producing heteroplasmy. During cell division and oogenesis, mitochondria segregate unevenly, so the mutant proportion varies among offspring and among tissues. Dysfunction becomes clinically apparent when the mutant load in a tissue exceeds that tissue's biochemical threshold, explaining marked intrafamilial and organ-specific variability.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Human mitochondrial DNA is transmitted almost exclusively through the mother; paternal mitochondrial transmission does not explain the pattern.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Anticipation from repeat expansion is a nuclear-genome mechanism and does not account for tissue-specific mutant mitochondrial fractions.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Genomic imprinting changes expression according to parental origin but does not produce variable percentages of mutant mitochondrial genomes among tissues.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: X-inactivation affects X-linked nuclear genes in individuals with more than one X chromosome and cannot explain mitochondrial heteroplasmy in both sexes.

questions.educational_objective: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy and random replicative segregation create variable mutant loads among tissues and relatives; disease appears when a tissue-specific threshold is exceeded.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing random mitochondrial segregation into daughter cells with different mutant loads and a threshold above which respiratory-chain dysfunction appears.
